column74: Hand Treatment, Cut Stump and Chemical Treatment of Siberian Elm, Saltcedar and Musk Thistle will be performed along the Canadian River Watershed partnering with US Forest Service and the Canadian River Riparian Restoration Project. The project is within an area that was previously treated by aerial application of herbicide using a helicopter equipped with GPS applying Amazapere to remove Saltcedar (which is not effective in the treatment of Siberian Elm); this follow up treatment using Cut Stump method and applying Garlon 4 (Triclopyr) to Elm and resprouts of Saltcedar and using Milestone (Amenopyralid) to treat Musk Thistle. The Canadian River Noxious Weed Treatment is a small portion of a larger watershed scale project which includes 8 Soil and Water Conservation Districts working together under a Joint Powers Agreement plus 21 state and federal agencies.

column84: The Ute Creek SWCD and Canadian River Riparian Restoration Project has a funding agreement with the US Forest Service to treat Saltcedar and other non-native invasives, also treat musk thistle and Siberian Elm completing restorative efforts and encouraging native vegetation and wild life to the Canadian River Watershed.
column87: The funding from this grant will be used to match federal funds to remove noxious weeds in the riparian areas along the Canadian River. This area of the Canadian River has been previously treated for non-native invasive species (Saltcedar) and now it requires follow-up treatment for Siberian Elm, Musk Thistle and resprouts of Saltcedar. This particular area of the Canadian River is the number 1 destination for "Bouldering" (Climbing Magazine) in the United States and is highly used for recreation, camping and hiking by the public.
column88: This project restores native vegetation to the Canadian River watershed and reduces water usage by non-native invasive species which benefits agricultural use, recreational use and creates additional wild life habitat. The Canadian River Watershed supplies water downstream to Conchas Lake and the Arch Hurley Irrigation District located in northeastern New Mexico. This in turn adds environmental benefit to the watershed while adding economic enhancement to all surrounding areas.
column89: We will be working in partnership with the US Forest Service on this Noxious Weed project. The US Forest Service will be providing $20,000.00 matching funds in support of this project as well as labor and personnel.
column90: This project provides additional treatment for remaining noxious weeds and ongoing maintenance for resprouts and seedlings.

column70: Integrated Weed Management (On-the-Ground Treatments) Planning, Capacity Development, and Partnership Building
column74: The Holmes property is on the East Side of the Rio Grande, directly across the river from Socorro, NM.  The property is bordered on the north by NMDGF land, and on the south by BLM (public) land.  This site is a popular place for local residents to sightsee, photograph, hunt, fish and enjoy easy access to the Rio Grande, made possible by the large arroyo running through the middle of it, and, more importantly, Mr. Holmes' desire to keep the land fully accessible.  Although it is his private land, he has allowed NMDGF to install signage, and he even installed a non-locking gate to ease access.  In 2007, the Socorro SWCD, using NMERD funding and state funding, contracted for 20.2 acres of non-native phreatophyte extraction and mulching.  Due to the infestation level, this left little vegetation remaining, save a small grove of old growth Rio Grande Cottonwood.  Following 7,220' of fencing, we planted 100 Rio Grande Cottonwood and Goodding's Black Willow trees, 250 assorted native shrubs, and broadcast 250 pounds of native grass seed.  The poles and shrub planting was aided by a soil salinity survey, helping us target the best spots for revegetation.  Following a wildfire in 2023, the property is now in need of fence repair, noxious species treatment, and further planting.

column74: To continue efforts towards restoration of riparian habitat impacted by the June 2017 Tiffany Fire, near San Marcial in Socorro County, Sierra SWCD, NM Ranch Properties, the Save Our Bosque Task Force, and New Mexico State Forestry have been working together to control noxious Saltcedar that became prevalent within the burn scar. Over the years since the fire, Saltcedar has been mechanically treated using grant dollars provided by various agencies including Water Trust Board and NM State Forestry. Mechanical treatment consisted of one of two methods: (1) mowing standing Saltcedar or (2) extracting Saltcedar with an excavator and mulching/spreading slash material. Areas that were mowed resulted in an increased number of resprouts compared to areas that were extracted. However, some locations within the project area could not be reached by any type of machinery due the number of down cottonwood skeletons caused by the fire. We plan to conduct a foliar application of herbicide during late September through early October. The selected contractor, will use an adaptive mixture of ground and aerial drone herbicide application. We would like to see continuous areas where harmful noxious weeds have been removed, allowing more desirable native plants to establish and thrive, thus restoring valuable riparian habitat. Sierra SWCD will host an education and outreach presentation that landowner and agency personnel will be invited to attend where they can see drone herbicide application and discuss the importance of responsibly treating noxious weeds.

column74:
The management and control of invasive species on Santa Clara Pueblo lands is a deemed priority and the Pueblo has already acquired and spent millions of dollars restoring riparian areas along the Rio Grande and Santa Clara Creek to protect riparian and wetland resources. Control efforts in other locations including agricultural fields along the Rio Grande have made a substantial difference. Although most large invasives have been removed, resprouting continues and the agricultural habitats need routine work to keep up with and improve the progress already made. 
For weed management on Santa Clara Pueblo, water stations include large capacity storage, pressurized systems, and underbody sprayers to be used at reducing invasive species spread and would ultimately save land managers hours of time for invasive weed removal. The timeline for our project begins in September of 2024 and will include seasonal weed removal activities 2 to 3 times throughout the fall and winter and early spring months which will conclude prior to June 30th, 2025. The Santa Clara Pueblo Department of Agriculture and Department of Forestry will be completing the field work within the areas of Santa Clara Pueblo.

column70: Survey and Mapping Integrated Weed Management (On-the-Ground Treatments)
column74:
Since 2007 the White Peak Landscape has been a focal area for forest restoration and fuels reduction, managed by the New Mexico State Land Office (NMSLO). Active forest management including forest thinning, prescribed fire, and removal of forest products have been essential to increasing ecosystem resilience to wildfire and reduce detrimental impacts of wildfire to the surrounding communities and watershed. Canada thistle has been persistent in presence and spread despite a robust native vegetation response following forest management activities. These noxious weeds have hindered the recovery of native species. While native vegetation is well adapted to frequent, low intensity fire at the project area, the presence of non-native, noxious plants shifts the competitive balance and creates a more undesirable understory composition following prescribed fires. 
NMSLO proposes to integrate yearly surveys and herbicide treatments into forest management activities. Over five years NMSLO will perform an annual pedestrian survey to detect and map occurrences of noxious weeds. Funds made available from this grant will help to provide the first year of treatments and mapping, kicking off a five-year total effort from NMSLO. Herbicide applications would be applied to targeted noxious species, with a focus on Canada thistle (Cirsium arvense), as well as musk thistle (Carduus nutans), Scotch thistle (Onopordum acanthium), and bull thistle (Cirsium vulgare). After a period of five years following effective treatments, management will shift, prioritizing early detection and treatment of subsequent occurrences. Following new forest management treatments,  heightened awareness and survey would take place for that specific treatment unit.

column88: Implementing thistle treatments throughout the project area will increase range productivity by reducing noxious weeds and in turn increasing native upland flora which would provide higher quality forage for wildlife and livestock. Herbicide treatments are highly cost effective and will yield a large treatment area as well as a high success rate in select thistle species, including Canada thistle is prevalent in the project area. Additionally, residents within surrounding communities may see a decrease in wildfire potential with decreased understory fuel loading due to reduced populations of dense thistle.

August/September 2024- One on the ground treatments begin, targeting Canada, musk, scotch, and bull thistle species. Herbicide will be applied utilizing 4-gallon backpack applicators with a crew of 4-12 individuals. Total treated acreage is 497 across the White Peak Landscape. 

September/October 2024- On the ground treatments to be completed notwithstanding weather conditions. If weather conditions do not permit finalizing treatments, herbicide application will be re-initiated in spring of 2025 when plants begin to grow and photosynthesize rapidly again. 

March-May 2025- Finalize any reaming treatments held over from initial on the ground treatments. Herbicide application will continue to target the above four species and will continue to follow herbicide application guidelines related to weather. 

Monitoring
Treatments are to be completed fall of 2024 and enter monitoring phase:
RME will conduct a one-month follow-up monitoring effort after completion of on the ground treatments. The one month follow-up will be to determine success rate of herbicide application. Two additional follow ups will be conducted in the March/April and May/June 2025 time frame, respectively. Spring 2025 follow up monitoring will be to determine success of Fall 2024 treatments and determine amount of new growth/regrowth throughout the project area.

Philmont Scout Ranch has a long-standing history of doing responsible and effective land management which includes extensive work with the Colfax County Soil and Water Conservation District to combat noxious weeds on Philmont Scout Ranch, Vermejo Park Ranch and the Valle Vidal.

Since 2023, Philmont has initiated restorative thinning plans in two units on the ranch covering a total of 900 acres. Within the Crater Restorative Thinning Unit ground disturbance from machinery has primed the area for higher-than-normal infestation of noxious weeds. Within the treatment unit there is a vast road and trail network along with stream channels that all can act as a mode for seed to rapidly disperse and move into other areas of lesser concern.  As part of a holistic land management approach, this project will address the need for treatment of know species in the unit (musk, bull and scotch thistle) and implement EDRR (hoary cress, yellow toadflax and canada thistle).  

The project area covers 420 acres in total which has been under ongoing treatment of noxious weeds for the past three years. Utilizing seasonal staff for herbicide treatments and conducting mechanical removal workdays with volunteer labor. A contract sprayer will be utilized to effectively treat the extensive acreage in this unit.

column74: In recent years the Gila National Forest (GNF) has been working with partner groups to complete invasive species surveys of the Wilderness areas it manages. 512 survey miles were completed in the Gila by partner group, Heart of the Gila. This project will use results of these surveys to target noxious weed treatments primarily in the Gila Wilderness. New Mexico Wild staff will be trained in Invasive species identification and physical removal methods. Focus species include Class A (yellow toadflax, camelthorn), Class B (bull thistle, poison hemlock), Class C (Siberian Elm, Eurasian watermilfoil, cheat grass).  Priorities will be identified with the GNF in early Spring, 2025, training begins in April, and five multiday backcountry hitches to conduct treatments will take place subsequently. The team will locate previous, spatially mapped infestations of Class A, B, and C species and complete treatments using established physical removal methods. If new infestations are found, they will be immediately surveyed with the Forest Service TESP-IS mobile application and then removed in an EDRR protocol. New infestations that can’t be immediately treated will be mapped. We will follow removal, EDRR, and survey guidelines laid out by USDA Forest Service-Southwestern region. The project also includes an education component consisting of four projects open to volunteers, who will help remove priority invasives. These projects will include sharing information from NMDA about detecting and treating early infestations of invasive plants, plus information about identifying priority noxious weeds. Post evaluation of treatments will be conducted by the GNF and partners.

column84: New Mexico Wild has cooperative agreements to assist the Forest Service with a wide array of project work, including work related to invasive species/noxious weeds, in Wilderness and wildlands on all five of the National Forests in New Mexico, including the Gila National Forest. One of the cooperative agreements is with the Gila National Forest and the second is with the Forest Service Regional Office, which allows work on National Forest System lands across NM. We also have verbal agreements and numerous email communications documenting this permission, as well as a support letter for this project from the Gila National Forest.
column87: The noxious weeds identified for removal in this project spread aggressively in riparian landscapes and areas of disturbance such as burn scars. Most infestations located within the Wilderness are along the Gila River, tributary streams, or in the Whitewater Baldy burn scar. It is critical to put resources into stopping the infestations of poison hemlock, bull thistle, yellow toadflax, and others before they spread throughout waterways and large disturbance areas. Providing funding for this effort will increase capacity to address emerging noxious weed issues and keep the infestations from becoming too large to feasibly manage. Maintaining the biodiversity of the Gila National Forest, and the Wilderness areas in particular, is a national, state, and local priority. Controlling invasive species in the upper watersheds of the river will help prevent movement of noxious weeds downstream into the farming communities of Gila and Cliff, NM, and support the outdoor recreation economy.
column88: The Gila River watershed is one of the most biodiverse networks of riparian areas in New Mexico that supports seven endangered species. Protecting the native riparian flora is critical to maintaining the habitat structure that supports these species.  It also provides one of the highest breeding bird concentrations in North America, including rare species such as the Gila Woodpecker and the threatened Southwestern Willow Flycatcher. Keeping this unique, biodiverse landscape intact aids in our efforts to combat climate change and stabilize New Mexico’s ecosystems. The characteristics of the Gila region contribute substantially to the regional tourist economy and maintaining wilderness character helps preserve the reasons people visit the area. This grant itself will generate new seasonal jobs that benefit young New Mexicans entering the work force. Controlling noxious weed infestations in headwaters areas will also prevent infestations downstream in agricultural areas, thereby avoiding potential economic impacts in agricultural communities.

HOTG has been working on invasive species management with the Gila since 2016 and recently completed a multi-year effort of 512 miles invasive species survey in the Gila. This will complement New Mexico Wild’s extensive experience managing backcountry crews and hosting educational events.

For logistical support, we will partner with local outfitter/guides like Gila Backcountry Services to provide implementation support in remote areas such as equipment and water drops, and where necessary, removal of noxious weed material.

Our 18-month proposal for Class B species focuses on African Rue, Spiny cockleburs and thistles.  Eighteen months can provide three Rue treatments; it is sprayed when in bloom in spring and fall.  The third treatment can take place September 2025.

2) Mapping & Education:  Provide trainings and materials to include, plant identification, detection and reporting of infestations using GPS, onX, Avenza and ArcGIS mapping.  Update existing maps as infestations are located and provide detailed treatment and reclamation data.  Coordinate with Extension Services to offer CEUs and herbicide application trainings.  
3) Integrate treatment plans:  Offer treatment cost-shares particularly for initial Rue treatment in September 2024.  Procurement procedures in place by October 2024 to complete RFPs enabling commercial applicator availability.  More applicators are now available in the area and have expressed interest in BSWCD’s Noxious Weed Program.
5) Establish reclamation plans:  Continuously monitor treated areas for timely reclamation practices. Offer cost-sharing for native seed, appropriate soil preparation materials like fertilizer and compost materials.  Documentation, photos, data sharing and on-site visits will be ongoing.
6) Strengthen partnerships:  Mapping, data sharing and treatments require statewide collaboration with agencies, SWCDs and CWMAs.  Our ultimate objective of landscape restoration naturally encourages teamwork.

  Many African Rue locations in BSWCD are known and demand immediate action and establishes us as a frontline in stopping its spread further into New Mexico.  Effective treatment of Rue takes place in spring and fall while in bloom.  These are especially busy times for ranchers.  Offering land managers a contracted applicator to help manage infestations can ensure cooperation, correct herbicide applications, use of restricted chemicals and more consistent treatments leading to successfully maintained reclamation of land and water.

column88:
Land managers are asking for help.  Noxious weeds are causing harm and/or death of livestock, overtaking areas of grassland and depleting groundwater.  This causes great economic hardship and our tax base suffers.  
  A few bites of African Rue can be fatal to humans or animals.  Its highly poisonous alkaloids kill quickly allowing little chance of recovery.  Cattle death losses create devastating economic impacts.  Wildlife losses cannot be calculated.
  Rue takes over large areas depleting groundwater.  It has a long tap root and spreads easily through rhizomes and prolific seeds.  Each chemical treatment kills only a portion of the root requiring years of constant management.  The window of opportunity to spray is only four to six weeks two times each year.  Mechanical removal attempts only stimulate growth.  It thrives on poor soil, so reclamation is costly and difficult.  Rue is a particularly dangerous and costly hazard in every way.

BSWCD’s evaluation of treated areas will remain constant allowing reclamation practices to be implemented under the right conditions for increased success rates.  Land managers will be encouraged to participate in the Healthy Soil Program (HSP) to expand access to reclamation needs.  Timely reclamation through seeding and proper soil preparation can give grass ample opportunity to establish and overtake the noxious weed populations over time.  Proper soil preparation practices will be evaluated to determine if compost, bale grazing or fertilizer is needed.
  African Rue poses a unique problem in that it prospers in poor soils; areas difficult for grasses to establish.  Land managers facing this problem will be encouraged to pursue HSP funding for extra resources to transition these soil types into grass-friendly areas.  Additionally, Rue flourishes in places such as oil well pads and in livestock pens where grass typically does not have opportunity to establish.  In these situations, continual monitoring for herbicide treatment can be recommended. 
  Providing land managers with cost-shared rental equipment such as seed broadcasters will also be offered.  This allows access to the appropriate equipment without our district having housing and maintenance responsibilities.  As our noxious weed program expands, we can seek purchasing a range of equipment for rental.
  The progress in each area will be logged with photo documentation and data added to existing maps.

column74: Taos Land Trust owns and maintains for public use a 20 acre park in Taos, adjacent to a 20 acre Taos municipal open space. We are active parciantes on the Vigil y Romo Acequia, which includes the Town of Taos and adjacent property owners of 5 additional acres in the project area. We will map, immediately address, and treat Class A, Class B, and Class C species that are prevalent on our property and adjacent sites for a total project area of 45 acres. We have begun mapping for Class A, Class B , and Class C species with a seasonal youth crew, and will augment that with mapping using staff time and GPS. For each species, we will identify two 30m X 30m plots with 3m X 3m subplots to monitor pre-and-post treatment inventory. Treatment methods include physical, mechanical, cultural, fire with individual blow torch applications, and chemical with high strength vinegar application. Commercial pesticides will not be used because we will be treating in an 8 acre wetlands area and 20 acres of the site is under a conservation easement. We will host public workshops to share our treatment results. For Siberian elm and Russian olive trees >10 inches, we will mill suitable material for use on the property, as a means to demonstrate possible commercial and artisanal uses for these woods. Work will take place between September 2024 and June 2025. Partners include the Town of Taos, Taos Land Trust, and the Vigil y Romo Acequia commission.

column74:
Luna County and the Deming Soil and Water Conservation District are concerned with the current infestations of African Rue, Malta Starthistle, Russian Knapweed, and Saltcedar within our county. These noxious and invasive plants reduce the agricultural, economical, and recreational value of the land.   Private landowners, public land users, and local governments and organizations must work together to implement this plan.

In order to achieve our goals, we will be utilizing an experienced contractor to treat these noxious species on public and private land.  Areas of high use will be targeted to reduce the spread of these plants from high volume vehicle and foot traffic.  There will be a strong focus on the treatment of roadways, right of ways, and public areas.  We will be monitoring the acres treated by evaluating current and past treatment areas and identifying areas of infestation that will require future herbicidal applications.

Our goal is to treat the noxious vegetation with herbicides on approximately 350 acres of private and public lands for the period of 9/24 – 11/25.  We will be monitoring these areas for re-infestation and treatment success. Documentation of methods and specific herbicides utilized are required of any contractor or individual who is applying the chemical treatment.  Specific location data (GPS coordinates) will also be required which will enable us to track areas of treatment and possible future reapplication.  Photos of these locations will be taken before and after chemical application to ensure that treatment efforts have been successful.

column87: Luna County has noxious and invasive plant infestations including African Rue, Malta Starthistle, Russian Knapweed, and Saltcedar that are adversely affecting the agricultural and recreational use of the land.  They are damaging the native plant population that is essential for wildlife habitat, watershed function, recreation, and livestock health. Human population growth is on the rise and it is substantially increasing the spread of these noxious plants.  The prolific and drought resistant nature of these plants allows them to spread rapidly and create dense plant populations that can cause a significant wildfire hazard during dry seasons. The cost of fighting these fires is substantial, as is the damage to native plant populations, wildlife habitats, valuable farm crops, residences, and businesses.  These invasive plants out-compete our native plant species for nutrients, sunlight, space, and water. Infestations need to be addressed immediately to prevent further and more permanent degradation of our lands.

Ranchers benefit from eliminating noxious plants on their private and leased lands by increasing native feeds necessary to provide optimal nutrition to their livestock. column92:
According to field research done by New Mexico State University, the most effective treatment and control of African Rue is with foliar active herbicides that can move deep into the plant’s elaborate root system.  While this method is the most effective, it can take up to a year for a plant to die.  Applying the herbicide in the spring and in the fall when the plant is in its growth stages is essential.  Herbicidal treatments have also proven effective for Malta Starthistle, Russian Knapweed, and Saltcedar and it allows for the largest coverage area while remaining cost efficient.

Deming Soil and Water Conservation District will provide a contractor to spray in early spring and late fall.  This contractor will be available to private landowners and public entities.  The contractor will be directed by and work closely with the Luna County Extension Service agent.  The contractor will be providing GPS coordinates of the areas treated to provide the most accurate representation of total acreage covered.  The documented areas of coverage will be assessed after each application to ensure that the treatment is effective.

column129:
A few smaller criticisms of this application could be distilled into the single criticism, that there are points where this application shies away from providing specific detail about the specific project. The project map, for example, is the entire Deming SWCD boundary, but one assumes that there's a specific 350 acres of project area in mind. And if there isn't a specific area in mind, but some sort of process for identifying where the contractor will be applied, then that process should be described. Similarly, the need and benefits are well written, but are described in very general terms. They didn't appear to reference a specific tract of land with a specific set of residents in mind. Many grants are reviewed by technical experts, and so while the background information about the species themselves is appreciated, it is often less functionally important than background information about the project itself. The connection to broader science and need is definitely important for selling the project, but the most important thing is for reviewers to understand and buy in to the project. 

Lastly, Deming SWCD is not a non-profit organization. It's is a governmental subdivision of the state (NMSA 73-20-44). Local governments, state governments, and even non-profits regularly find match to make grant applications more competitive so they can receive grant money. If the district doesn't have funds, for lack of grants or a mill levy or tax base (human population is not growing in Luna county), then that is entirely valid and can/should be explained.
